newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Bills flatten, durations extended.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Bills flatten, durations extended.

text.p: While the spread between yields of U.S. Treasury two-year notes to 30-year bonds remains steady, the front end of the yield curve has flattened substantially as the market no longer expects a near-term Federal Reserve tightening.

Over the past week or so, six-month and one-year bill rates have fallen as three-month bill rates have barely budged. Whereas the six-month to three-month bill spread was eight basis points just two weeks ago and as little as six basis points last week, the spread Tuesday morning was zero.

Further, the one-year to three-month spread has narrowed to 19 basis points from 26 a couple of weeks ago. Over the same period, the spread between the two-year note and one-year bill has also flattened on a yield basis to 35 basis points from about 45.

Traders said much of the focus of the bill curve has centered on the six-month bill, which -- on a discount rate basis -- has dipped to 4.97 percent from 5.07 last week. The three-month meanwhile, was also at 4.97 percent, from 5.00 percent.
Earlier Tuesday, the curve inverted briefly, as the six-month bill fell to 4.95 percent, while the three-month bill was at 4.96 percent.

"Foreign central banks are buying six-month paper and holding it," said one trader at a U.S. primary dealership and echoed by another trader. "What we have been seeing the last couple days is people extending out the curve."
U.S. retail accounts are also said to be big buyers of six-month bills.
However, traders noted liquidity in bills is very low, exaggerating price moves somewhat.

Indeed, while trading volume in outstanding bills was a combined $1.5 billion late morning on Tuesday, the two-, three- and 10-year notes had volume above $2.0 billion each, with the five-year note at $3.4 billion, according to GovPX.
And, while bill rates have come down 10 basis points, the yield on the long bond is more than 20 basis points lower in recent sessions.

"When the market trades well, people try and reach out for yield," explained another trader at a U.S. bank. "We are in the process of taking the Fed out of the equation for another couple months so there is little upside left" for three-month bills.
With fears for a tightening allayed for now, some traders expect the bill curve to flatten further in the near future, with the six-month and year-bills declining another 10 basis points.

"We're fully priced for federal funds staying at 5.25 percent for the long term," said a bill trader at a Japanese-based dealer. "Some say maybe we won't have a tightening; the strength of the dollar will keep prices down."
In addition, he said the market believes petroleum prices have "topped out," resulting in more favorable inflation data.
Three-month bills, though, won't fall out of bed, traders said, since some conservative funds have invested heavily in tht sector.

Yet, traders said they were not optimistic about prospects for a successful three- and six-month bill auction later Tuesday afternoon. Given the holiday on Monday, the market has one day less to trade the new when-issued bills.
Therefore, traders said, dealers will buy the new bills today but roll them over once details of Monday's auction are announced an hour or so later.
In when-issued trading at around 1150 EST/1650 GMT, the three-month was at 4.98 percent and the six-month was at 5.03 percent.
